news.title: Teknoloji hisseleri düşerken Wall Street fırsat görüyor: İşte öne çıkan şirketler
news.summary: ABD ara seçimlerinin ardından teknoloji hisselerinde yaşanan sert düşüşler, Wall Street'in önde gelen kurumlarının gündeminde. Morgan Stanley, UBS ve HSBC, yapay zeka sektörüne yönelik büyüme beklentilerini korurken son satışların alım fırsatı yaratabileceğine işaret etti.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Teknoloji hisseleri düşerken Wall Street fırsat görüyor: İşte öne çıkan şirketler
news.summaryTr: ABD ara seçimlerinin ardından teknoloji hisselerinde yaşanan sert düşüşler, Wall Street'in önde gelen kurumlarının gündeminde. Morgan Stanley, UBS ve HSBC, yapay zeka sektörüne yönelik büyüme beklentilerini korurken son satışların alım fırsatı yaratabileceğine işaret etti.
news.articleText: Teknoloji hisseleri düşerken Wall Street fırsat görüyor: İşte öne çıkan şirketler ABD ara seçimlerinin ardından teknoloji hisselerinde yaşanan sert düşüşler, Wall Street'in önde gelen kurumlarının gündeminde. Morgan Stanley, UBS ve HSBC, yapay zeka sektörüne yönelik büyüme beklentilerini korurken son satışların alım fırsatı yaratabileceğine işaret etti. ABD'de ara seçimlerin ardından Demokratların Kongre'de kontrolü ele geçirmesi, yapay zeka sektörüne yönelik düzenlemelerin sıkılaşabileceği endişelerini artırdı. Özellikle veri merkezi yatırımlarının geleceğine ilişkin belirsizlikler, teknoloji hisselerinde satış baskısını beraberinde getirdi. Ancak Wall Street'in önde gelen finans kuruluşları, piyasalardaki sert tepkinin sektörün temel dinamikleriyle örtüşmediği görüşünde birleşiyor. Analistler, olası düzenlemelerin yapay zeka yatırımlarını durdurmaktan çok projelerin hayata geçirilme takvimini etkileyebileceğini düşünüyor. Morgan Stanley'den veri merkezi yatırımları için dikkat çeken tahmin Morgan Stanley, seçimlerin ardından veri merkezi projelerinin sekteye uğrayacağı endişesiyle teknoloji hisselerinde yaşanan değer kayıplarını aşırı buldu. Kurumun analizine göre, ABD'de 2028 yılında devreye alınması planlanan yaklaşık 5 gigavatlık veri merkezi kapasitesi, düzenleyici süreçler nedeniyle bir yıl gecikerek 2029'a sarkabilir. Bununla birlikte söz konusu ertelemenin, büyük bulut bilişim şirketlerinin toplam yatırım harcamalarında belirgin bir azalmaya yol açması beklenmiyor. Morgan Stanley analistleri, projelerin daha uzun bir döneme yayılmasının sektörde olumlu sonuçlar da doğurabileceğine dikkat çekti. Yatırımların zamana yayılmasıyla arz ve talep arasındaki dengenin güçlenebileceği, finansman koşullarının iyileşebileceği ve veri merkezi kapasitesinin kiralama bedellerinin yükselebileceği değerlendiriliyor. Nvidia, Amazon ve Alphabet hisseleri öne çıkıyor Morgan Stanley, teknoloji hisselerindeki geri çekilmeyi yatırım fırsatı olarak görmeye devam ediyor. Kurumun olumlu değerlendirdiği büyük teknoloji şirketleri arasında Amazon, Meta Platforms ve Alphabet bulunuyor. Yapay zeka altyapısına yönelik yatırımlardan yararlanabilecek şirketler arasında ise çip üreticileri Nvidia ve Broadcom öne çıkıyor. Veri depolama alanında Seagate ve Western Digital, optik iletişim teknolojilerinde de Coherent ve Lumentum, Morgan Stanley'nin fırsat gördüğü şirketler arasında yer alıyor. Gözler Nvidia'nın bilançosuna çevrildi Wall Street analistlerine göre yapay zeka hisselerinin kısa vadeli performansında, Washington'dan gelecek düzenleme haberlerinin yanı sıra şirketlerin finansal sonuçları da önemli rol oynayacak. Bu kapsamda yatırımcıların odağında Nvidia'nın 17 Kasım'da ABD borsalarının kapanışından sonra açıklaması beklenen üçüncü çeyrek bilançosu bulunuyor. Piyasa beklentileri, şirketin veri merkezi faaliyetlerinden elde ettiği gelirlerin önceki çeyreğe kıyasla yüzde 12'den fazla büyüyeceğine işaret ediyor. Nvidia'nın açıklayacağı sonuçların, yapay zeka altyapısına yönelik güçlü talebin sürüp sürmediğine ilişkin önemli sinyaller vermesi bekleniyor. HSBC teknoloji hisselerinde pozisyon artırdı HSBC ise son dönemde yaşanan fiyat düşüşlerini portföyünde değişikliğe gitmek için kullandı. Kurum, geçen haftaki satışların ardından hem ABD hem de Asya piyasalarındaki teknoloji şirketlerine yönelik yatırımlarını artırdığını duyurdu. HSBC'nin değerlendirmesinde, önümüzdeki haftalarda yapay zeka sektöründe fiyatlamaları etkileyebilecek gelişmeler arasında Anthropic'in beklenen halka arzı öne çıkarıldı. UBS: Yatırımcılar riskleri olduğundan büyük görüyor UBS de yapay zeka sektörüne ilişkin piyasa endişelerinin aşırı boyutlara ulaştığı görüşünü paylaştı. Kurumun analistleri, siyasi düzenlemeler, şirketlerin borçlanma koşulları ve yüksek yatırım harcamalarının sürdürülebilirliği konusunda yatırımcıların gereğinden fazla kötümser davrandığını belirtti. Jefferies analisti Jane Gibbons da 5 Kasım'da yaşanan satış dalgasının, yapay zeka sektörünün uzun vadeli görünümünde köklü bir bozulmadan ziyade kısa süreli bir piyasa tepkisi olarak değerlendirilmesi gerektiğini ifade etti. Gibbons, geçmiş piyasa hareketlerine işaret ederek S&P 500 endeksinin bir günde yüzde 4'ten fazla gerilediği dönemlerin ardından, takip eden altı ayda ortalama yüzde 11,9'luk toparlanma yaşandığını aktardı. Analiste göre aynı dönemleri izleyen 12 aylık süreçte ortalama yükseliş yüzde 20'yi aştı. Bununla birlikte geçmiş performansın gelecekte benzer getirileri garanti etmediği unutulmamalı. Wall Street'te uzun vadeli büyüme beklentisi korunuyor Yatırım kuruluşlarının analizlerinde ortak görüş, ABD'deki siyasi gelişmelerin yapay zeka yatırımlarının büyüme potansiyelini ortadan kaldırmayacağı yönünde şekilleniyor. Demokratların kontrolündeki Kongre'nin olası düzenlemeleri bazı veri merkezi projelerinde gecikmelere neden olabilecek olsa da büyük teknoloji şirketlerinin yapay zeka altyapısına yönelik harcamalarını sürdürmesi bekleniyor. Bu nedenle Wall Street'te son satış dalgasının kalıcı bir trend değişiminden çok, güçlü büyüme beklentileri devam eden sektörde bir düzeltme hareketi olabileceği görüşü ağırlık kazanıyor.

news.summary: ABD'li çip devi Nvidia ve CEO'su Jensen Huang hakkında, Çin istihbaratıyla bağlantılı olduğu öne sürülen bir iş insanıyla ilişkilerin gizlenerek yatırımcıların yanıltıldığı iddiasıyla dava açıldı. Şirket hisseleri yüzde 4,27 değer kaybetti.

news.titleTr: Nvidia'da casusluk krizi büyüyor: Yatırımcılar dava açtı
news.summaryTr: ABD'li çip devi Nvidia ve CEO'su Jensen Huang hakkında, Çin istihbaratıyla bağlantılı olduğu öne sürülen bir iş insanıyla ilişkilerin gizlenerek yatırımcıların yanıltıldığı iddiasıyla dava açıldı. Şirket hisseleri yüzde 4,27 değer kaybetti.
news.articleText: Nvidia'da casusluk krizi büyüyor: Yatırımcılar dava açtı - ABD'li çip devi Nvidia ve CEO'su Jensen Huang hakkında, Çin istihbaratıyla bağlantılı olduğu öne sürülen bir iş insanıyla ilişkilerin gizlenerek yatırımcıların yanıltıldığı iddiasıyla dava açıldı. Şirket hisseleri yüzde 4,27 değer kaybetti. ABD merkezli teknoloji devi Nvidia ve şirketin Üst Yöneticisi (CEO) Jensen Huang hakkında, yatırımcıları yanıltıcı açıklamalarda bulundukları iddiasıyla dava açıldı. Davanın merkezinde, Huang'ın Çin adına istihbarat faaliyetleri yürüttüğünden şüphelenilen Singapur merkezli Megaspeed şirketinin eski yöneticisi Alice Huang ile ilişkisi yer alıyor. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle California Kuzey Bölge Mahkemesine sunulan dava dilekçesinde, Nvidia ve CEO'sunun yatırımcıları ilgilendiren önemli bilgileri kamuoyundan gizlediği ve bu nedenle ABD'nin 1934 tarihli Menkul Kıymetler Borsası Kanunu'nu ihlal ettiği ileri sürüldü. Yatırımcıları yanıltma suçlaması Davacı taraf, Nvidia'nın ürettiği çiplerin Çin'e yönlendirildiğine ilişkin herhangi bir kanıt bulunmadığı yönündeki açıklamalarının gerçeği tam olarak yansıtmadığını savundu. Jensen Huang'ın Megaspeed ile ticari ilişkilerini olağan iş faaliyetleri kapsamında değerlendiren ifadeleri de dava dilekçesinde tartışma konusu oldu. Dilekçede, Huang'ın Çin istihbaratıyla bağlantılı olduğu iddia edilen Alice Huang ile ilişkisini açıklamamasının yatırımcıların şirketin karşı karşıya bulunduğu riskleri doğru değerlendirmesini engellediği öne sürüldü. Söz konusu bilgilerin Nvidia'nın itibarını, ulusal güvenlik alanındaki konumunu ve gelecekteki ticari faaliyetlerini etkileyebileceğini belirten davacılar, yatırımcıların uğradığı zararların tazmin edilmesini istedi. Nvidia bağımsız soruşturma başlattı Dava, Nvidia yönetiminin Jensen Huang hakkındaki iddiaları araştırmak üzere harekete geçmesinin ardından gündeme geldi. Şirketin Yönetim Kurulu, 8 Kasım'da yaptığı açıklamada, Huang'ın yabancı istihbarat faaliyetlerinin hedefi olabileceğine yönelik haberler üzerine bağımsız soruşturma başlatıldığını duyurmuştu. The New York Times'ın haberlerinde, Huang ile yakın ilişkisi bulunduğu belirtilen Megaspeed'in eski yöneticisi Alice Huang'ın Çin istihbaratı adına faaliyet yürüttüğü ve Pekin yönetimine bilgi aktardığı iddia edilmişti. Jensen Huang'dan çalışanlarına açıklama İddiaların kamuoyuna yansımasının ardından Nvidia CEO'su Jensen Huang, şirket çalışanlarına gönderdiği mesajda özel hayatına ilişkin açıklamalarda bulunmuştu. Eşine sadık kalmadığını kabul eden Huang, Yönetim Kurulunun başlattığı bağımsız soruşturmaya destek verdiğini ve süreç boyunca tam işbirliği yapacağını ifade etmişti. Huang, Nvidia'nın çıkarlarını koruma ve ABD'nin ulusal güvenliğini destekleme konusundaki kararlılığını da vurgulamıştı. Nvidia hisselerinde yüzde 4'ü aşan kayıp Şirket yönetimine yönelik iddialar ve başlatılan soruşturma, Nvidia hisseleri üzerinde de baskı oluşturdu. ABD borsalarında 9 Kasım'da Nvidia hisseleri yüzde 4,27 değer kaybederek günü 178,67 dolardan tamamladı. Açılan davada yer alan suçlamalar henüz mahkeme tarafından karara bağlanmazken, bağımsız soruşturmanın sonuçları ve hukuki sürecin seyri yatırımcılar tarafından yakından takip ediliyor.

Bir önceki gün yüzde 1’den fazla yükselen değerli metalde yatırımcıların kâr realizasyonuna yönelmesi, fiyatlar üzerinde aşağı yönlü baskı oluşturdu. Reuters’a konuşan Capital.com Kıdemli Finans Piyasaları Analisti Kyle Rodda, piyasadaki hareketin sınırlı olduğunu belirterek fiyatların ABD işlem seansında ulaştığı zirvelerden geri çekildiğini ve bunun kâr satışlarından kaynaklanabileceğini söyledi. Trump’ın İran açıklaması altın fiyatları açısından önem taşıyor Rodda, ABD’nin Ortadoğu’daki çatışmayı tırmandırmaktan kaçınması ve petrol fiyatlarında düşüş yaşanması durumunda bunun altını destekleyebileceğini belirtti. Analiste göre petrol fiyatlarındaki gerilemenin dolar, enflasyon ve faiz oranlarına ilişkin beklentiler üzerindeki etkisi, değerli metal açısından olumlu bir zemin oluşturabilir. ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, pazartesi günü yaptığı açıklamada, bölge ülkelerinin talepleri doğrultusunda İran’a yönelik yeni askeri saldırıları şimdilik ertelemeyi planladığını söyledi. Trump, Katar Başbakanı’nın Beyaz Saray’daki görüşmeler sırasında yaptığı çağrıların da bu kararda etkili olduğunu belirtti. Fed yetkilisinden enflasyon uyarısı Richmond Fed Başkanı Tom Barkin, pazartesi günü yaptığı açıklamada, ABD Merkez Bankası’nın enflasyona karşı izleyeceği politikayı dikkatli biçimde yürütmesi gerektiğini söyledi. Enflasyonun merkez bankası açısından en büyük risk olmaya devam ettiğini belirten Barkin, aralık ayındaki toplantıda alınması gereken karara ilişkin belirgin bir temel senaryosu bulunmadığını ifade etti. CME FedWatch verilerine göre yatırımcılar, Fed’in aralık ayında faiz artırma olasılığını yüzde 84 olarak fiyatlıyor. Bu oran bir hafta önce yaklaşık yüzde 74 seviyesindeydi. Faiz oranlarının yüksek seyretmesi, faiz getirisi sağlamayan altın gibi varlıkları elde tutmanın fırsat maliyetini artırıyor. Bu durum, değerli metalin yatırımcılar açısından cazibesini azaltan unsurlar arasında yer alıyor. Piyasaların odağında ABD TÜFE ve ÜFE verileri var Yatırımcılar, Fed’in faiz politikasına ilişkin beklentileri şekillendirebilecek ABD enflasyon göstergelerini takip ediyor. Günün ilerleyen saatlerinde açıklanacak tüketici fiyat endeksi (TÜFE) verisinin ardından piyasaların odağında cuma günü yayımlanacak üretici fiyat endeksi (ÜFE) bulunuyor. Gram altının satış fiyatı ne kadar? Bu gelişmelerle birlikte yurt içinde altının gram alış fiyatı 6.606,02 ve satış fiyatı 6.652,52 TL oldu. Gram altın fiyatı, küresel piyasalarda ons altının dolar bazındaki değerinin dolar/TL kuruyla birleşmesi ve yurt içi piyasa koşullarının bu bileşime yansımasıyla oluşur.

news.titleTr: Vergi borcu olanların isimleri açıklanacak: 5 milyon TL sınırı
news.summaryTr: Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığı, 5 milyon TL ve üzerinde vergi borcu veya kesinleşmiş vergi ve cezası bulunan mükelleflerin kamuoyuna açıklanmasına karar verdi. Vergi borçlularının listeleri aralık ayında önce vergi dairelerinde, ardından Gelir İdaresi Başkanlığının internet sitesinde yayımlanacak.
news.articleText: Vergi borcu olanların isimleri açıklanacak: 5 milyon TL sınırı - Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığı, 5 milyon TL ve üzerinde vergi borcu veya kesinleşmiş vergi ve cezası bulunan mükelleflerin kamuoyuna açıklanmasına karar verdi. Vergi borçlularının listeleri aralık ayında önce vergi dairelerinde, ardından Gelir İdaresi Başkanlığının internet sitesinde yayımlanacak. Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığı, yüksek tutarlı vergi borcu ve cezalarına ilişkin kamuoyuna açıklama yapılmasının esaslarını belirledi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Gelir İdaresi Başkanlığı tarafından hazırlanan Vergi Usul Kanunu Genel Tebliği (Sıra No: 597), 10 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanarak yürürlüğe girdi. Yeni düzenlemeyle, kesinleşmiş vergi ve cezaları belirlenen tutarın üzerinde olan veya vadesi geçtiği halde vergi borcunu ödemeyen mükelleflerin kamuoyuna açıklanmasının önü açıldı. 5 milyon TL sınırı uygulanacak Tebliğe göre, her bir vergi dairesi bazında 5 milyon TL ve üzerinde ödenmemiş vergi borcu bulunan mükellefler açıklanacak. Aynı tutarda veya daha yüksek kesinleşmiş vergi ve cezası bulunanlar da listelerde yer alacak. Borç listeleri hazırlanırken 31 Aralık 2025 itibarıyla vadesi dolmuş ancak 20 Kasım 2026 tarihine kadar ödenmemiş vergi ve cezalar esas alınacak. Bunun yanı sıra 1 Haziran 2025 ile 31 Mayıs 2026 tarihleri arasında kesinleşen vergi tarhiyatları da kamuoyuna duyurulacak. Vergi borçlularının isimleri aralık ayında yayımlanacak Düzenleme kapsamında hazırlanan listeler iki aşamada açıklanacak. İlk aşamada, 1-15 Aralık 2026 tarihleri arasında mükelleflere ilişkin bilgiler Türkiye genelindeki vergi dairelerinin ilan alanlarında yayımlanacak. İkinci aşamada ise 16-30 Aralık 2026 tarihleri arasında listeler Gelir İdaresi Başkanlığının resmî internet sitesinden erişime açılacak. Böylece belirlenen sınırın üzerinde vergi borcu veya kesinleşmiş vergi cezası bulunan mükelleflerin bilgileri kamuoyuyla paylaşılmış olacak.

news.title: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
news.summary: The president says the US is keeping "status quo" with Iran but remains “locked and loaded” should the situation in the Middle East change.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
news.summaryTr: The president says the US is keeping "status quo" with Iran but remains “locked and loaded” should the situation in the Middle East change.
news.articleText: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely' - Published Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict. "We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours." Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change. Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict. This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now. The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war. Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict. Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression. "We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure. Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war. In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region". Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region. Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration. Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him. Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham". While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate. - Published3 hours ago - Published2 days ago

news.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
news.summary: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
news.summaryTr: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
news.articleText: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy - Published US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy. Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China". Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off its value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%. Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the investigation, or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang. According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. - What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - Published5 hours ago Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia. Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage. Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday. The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team. The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment. Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns. Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy. The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China." The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit. 'He said he had no idea she was a spy' At the White House, Trump was asked several times, including by the BBC, when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific. Trump said he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations. "I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added. He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy". Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities. The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met. Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched. Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear. A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang". Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees. - Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published7 hours ago - AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values - Published3 days ago Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company. Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent. It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today. Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold. The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions. Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market. Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China". Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off its value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%. Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the investigation, or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang. According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. - What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - Published5 hours ago Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia. Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage. Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday. The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team. The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment. Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns. Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy. The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China." The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit. 'He said he had no idea she was a spy' At the White House, Trump was asked several times, including by the BBC, when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific. Trump said he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations. "I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added. He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy". Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities. The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met. Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched. Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear. A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang". Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees. - Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published7 hours ago - AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values - Published3 days ago Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company. Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent. It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today. Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold. The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions. Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market. news.titleTr: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
news.summaryTr: The Australian airline said the move was aimed at modernising its IT systems and noted the impact of AI.
news.articleText: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India - Published Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment. In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings". The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems. Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans. The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs. On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient". Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded. "Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said. The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business". The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI". Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia. Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work. The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

news.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
news.summary: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process next year.

news.titleTr: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
news.summaryTr: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process next year.
news.articleText: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth - Published A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution. "By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said. The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process. Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record. "You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down." He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda. Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside. "I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles. Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power. "My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials." Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January. Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that". He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject. President Trump has indicated that he plans to stick by Hegseth, praising his leadership in the US capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year and defending his work during the war in Iran. "We've made the world a lot safer place. Why haven't we gone after all these other people that ran wars and lost?" Trump said on Monday at the White House. He also touted recruitment numbers under Hegseth. "The soldiers, the actual soldiers, the great people that do the work, the great patriots, they love Pete Hegseth," he said. "He's done a very good job." Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed. As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict. The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one. While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago. He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years. Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority. Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins. "There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said. Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House. While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term. When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 60 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office. Related topics - Published1 day ago

news.title: HIVE, MARA mine more Bitcoin but earn less as crypto prices fall
news.summary: Both miners reported higher Bitcoin production but lower mining revenue and rising electricity costs as they expanded their AI infrastructure businesses.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: HIVE, MARA mine more Bitcoin but earn less as crypto prices fall
news.summaryTr: Both miners reported higher Bitcoin production but lower mining revenue and rising electricity costs as they expanded their AI infrastructure businesses.
news.articleText: HIVE, MARA mine more Bitcoin but earn less as crypto prices fall Both miners reported higher Bitcoin production but lower mining revenue and rising electricity costs as they expanded their AI infrastructure businesses. HIVE Digital Technologies and MARA Holdings mined more Bitcoin in the September quarter than a year earlier but reported lower mining revenue, as weaker Bitcoin prices outweighed gains in production. According to their latest regulatory filings, HIVE’s Bitcoin production increased 49% to 1,070 Bitcoin (BTC), while mining revenue fell 7.4% to $76 million. MARA reported a similar pattern, with production rising 5% to 2,247 BTC and Bitcoin mining revenue dropping 34% to $159 million. Both companies reported higher power bills and equipment charges. HIVE’s electricity costs rose 20% to $45.6 million, while MARA’s purchased energy costs increased 12% to $48.1 million as it expanded its owned mining operations. HIVE also recorded a $31.2 million noncash write-down on mining equipment, citing “depressed mining economics,” while MARA separately wrote off $12 million involving mining rigs and equipment under restructuring plans. Both results add to signs of pressure on Bitcoin mining economics. American Bitcoin last week reported weaker mining margins despite a treasury-driven quarterly profit, while Core Scientific said it plans to leave mining entirely by year-end. HIVE and MARA expand AI businesses alongside mining Unlike Core Scientific, HIVE and MARA are both continuing to invest in Bitcoin mining alongside artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. HIVE’s HPC hosting revenue rose 71% to $8.8 million in the September quarter, accounting for 10.4% of total revenue. The company has described its strategy as combining cash flow from mining with recurring revenue from AI infrastructure. Related: American Bitcoin’s $126M profit masks mining pressure as rivals turn to AI HIVE said it anticipates spending up to $493 million over 36 months to expand its HPC operations, including acquiring land, building out data center infrastructure and buying up GPUs. The company reported spending $145.3 million toward that expansion as of the filing. HIVE also plans to spend about $35 million converting its Toronto facility into a Tier-III data center. Meanwhile, it continues to expand its mining infrastructure, targeting a 100-megawatt substation expansion at its Yguazú site in Paraguay during 2026. MARA is also developing AI infrastructure through its Exaion subsidiary and a partnership with Starwood Digital Ventures. It said it intends to operate sites that can shift between workloads depending on economics, demand and grid conditions, with Bitcoin mining remaining the foundation of its platform. Treasury gains lift MARA profit, HIVE reports quarterly loss HIVE’s Nasdaq-listed shares fell 1.7% to $1.78 in after-hours trading Monday, according to Google Finance, after closing the regular session up 1.7% at $1.81. The company reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $84.9 million, down 2.7% from a year earlier but above the $79.4 million consensus estimate listed by MarketBeat. Meanwhile, MARA reported net income attributable to common stockholders of $634.4 million, up from $123.1 million a year earlier, and included substantial fair-value gains on digital assets and digital asset receivables. MARA reported quarterly revenue of $164.2 million, down 35% year-on-year, and diluted earnings of $1.28 a share, up from 27 cents, while its shares were little changed at $6.64 in after-hours trading Monday after closing up 4.6%. news.title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
news.summary: The BBC hears from Vinted sellers who describe difficulties accessing money held in their online wallets.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
news.summaryTr: The BBC hears from Vinted sellers who describe difficulties accessing money held in their online wallets.
news.articleText: I took Vinted to court to get my money back - Published Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000. She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter. But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action. Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team. Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there. After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets. Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business. This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business. Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process. "I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed." Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses. In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted. After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees. 'I need that cash' Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds. She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest. In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50. But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December. "It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says. "I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me." Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified." The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue. Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters." 'It's not right' Sportswear seller Azri Mukthar told the BBC he has been trying to withdraw almost £2,500 from his account for over a year. news.titleTr: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor
news.summaryTr: A woman says an agency boss sent her to photoshoots at the sex offender's Florida beach home.
news.articleText: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor - Published A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house. At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home. "My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service. Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models. "My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza. She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house. She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women. Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her. Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused. We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction. The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company. Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates. A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie. He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers. Sara Ziff, founder of the Model Alliance, which campaigns for stronger protections for models in the US, approves. "Often, [model agencies] are the problem. They are the link between the model and these predatory men." Roza says the person behind the camera at the photoshoots MC2 sent her to was not a professional photographer, but Epstein's girlfriend at the time, Nadia Marcinko. Roza describes the set-up as "strange - there was no stylist" and the photos were never used. She has since become convinced the shoots were stage-managed by Epstein and MC2. The Model Trap BBC Eye reveals new evidence showing how scouts, agencies and powerful fashion figures helped Jeffrey Epstein gain access to young women after his conviction for sex offences. If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, external An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier. "Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says. A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency. We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply. Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims. "Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked." In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school. The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse. Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein. We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse. Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed." He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual." - If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves. "These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do." Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times. "People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona. She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates. At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company. Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein. After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling. And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years. The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place. Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him." They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery. We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply. Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable". Roza hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward. "There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out." Additional reporting by Annika Grosser

news.summary: Kyiv, Washington and Moscow are all sending delegation to the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.

news.titleTr: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
news.summaryTr: Kyiv, Washington and Moscow are all sending delegation to the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.
news.articleText: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say - Published Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said. The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February. Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches. Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine. "An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X. But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart. A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia. Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security. While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately". However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture". "They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other." For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans. The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022. The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since. Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks. The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans." Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success. Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union. After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe". Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace. Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv. The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said. "While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war". Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky. Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya. Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms. On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations." "This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism." news.titleTr: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
news.summaryTr: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
news.articleText: A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise. In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON. For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared. Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011. And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK. As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between. America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels. Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet. The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills? Two decisions On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil. Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security. Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas. Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations. Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable. At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama. But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt." "We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy." There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it. The case for drilling Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!" Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field. Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks. The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills". "If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice. Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress. But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets." Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had." Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead. Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption. And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another. With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination. The case for electrons The alternative is to build. Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel. The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables. The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs. Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power. And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills. All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills. The China question And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars. And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember. The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on. I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market". Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said. Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering. "There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was. Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs. Foreign investment, then - just not from China. Role reversal Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C. China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early. And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo. If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.
